title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
This document gives an overview of how bases work in Rust: the Tool Cupboard (TC) and building privilege, upkeep and decay, doors and locks, a short tour of deployables, and the fundamentals of raiding with explosives and siege tools. It is a foundation: it explains the shape of the systems and points to deeper documents rather than listing every value.

The headline is that a base must be kept supplied through its TC or it decays, that the monthly updates keep changing the upkeep rules (a group upkeep tax arrived in September 2026), and that raid costs change with balance passes. Confidence is Medium: the mechanics come from the Facepunch wiki and devblogs, but the wiki's Tool Cupboard page is undated, hit-point tables were not obtainable from an openable source, and offline-raiding behaviour could not be sourced.
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
- A Tool Cupboard costs 1000 wood to craft; without one a base decays and other players can build on it [2].
- Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment drawn from the TC inventory; with no resources in the TC, decay begins immediately [2].
- The wiki lists decay timers after the matching material runs out: twig 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours (wiki page undated; check in game) [2].
- From the September 2026 update, TCs add a group upkeep tax: the first 4 players pay none, the next 6 add 2% each, later players 4% each, capped at 300% [3].
- Code locks use a four-digit code and cost 100 metal fragments; key locks cost 75 wood [4][5].
- A Timed Explosive Charge (C4) is crafted from 20 explosives, 5 cloth and 2 tech trash at Workbench Level 3 [6].
- The latest update checked, the Livestock Update (1 October 2026), made no upkeep change but fixed a battering ram bug that hit TCs through walls [1].

text:
- **Tool Cupboard (TC):** the deployable that grants building privilege and holds upkeep resources [2].
- **Building privilege:** authorisation to build and pick up deployables within the TC area [2].
- **Upkeep:** the periodic resource payment, a fraction of build cost, drawn from the TC [2].
- **Honeycomb:** multiple layers of walls placed to make raiding through that side more expensive [7].
- **Airlock:** two or more opposing doors within a single foundation [7].
- **Footprint:** the layout of a base's foundations [7].
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
**Building privilege.** Placing a TC authorises the placer. Authorised players can build and pick up deployables in the radius and can set off flame and shotgun traps; others press E at the TC to authorise, and an authorised player can deauthorise by holding E. Anyone with access can hold E to clear every authorised player [2]. The privilege area is projected from the connected foundations, not from the TC position [2]. Unauthorised players can still place twig floors and wooden ladders, shown as an orange "BUILDING BLOCKED" outline; other placements show red [2]. Separate buildings each need their own TC coverage [2].

**Upkeep.** Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment, a fraction of the build cost, taken from the TC inventory. Walls, foundations, ceilings, roofs, doors and window pieces contribute; items inside the base such as sleeping bags do not. A stone base with sheet metal doors consumes only stone and metal fragments. Remaining protection time shows in the TC inventory [2]. High external walls add no upkeep and are protected within a TC's radius; small "external" TCs can cover walls outside the main radius [2].

**Decay.** Once a material runs out in the TC, parts made of it decay: twig after 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours. Decay starts at the outermost exposed layers and works inward, and only parts of the exhausted material decay [2]. A destroyed TC holding resources consumes up to 24 hours of upkeep, protecting the base for 24 hours from that point [2].

**Group upkeep tax.** Since the September 2026 update, TCs add an upkeep tax based on the number of players in the base. Counted players are those authorised on the TC or a code lock (guest codes included) plus those deauthorised from either in the last 24 hours. Server owners can adjust or disable it through ConVars in the Decay class [3].

**Doors and locks.** The code lock opens with a four-digit code [4]. The key lock is placed on a door and keys can be shared with friends [5]. The armoured door is described as an extremely strong door with a hatch to see and shoot out of [8]. Doors are one input to base design alongside honeycomb and airlock layouts [7].

**Deployables overview.** The Facepunch wiki groups base-related items as doors and locks, barricades, walls and windows, and raiding tools [9]. The Livestock Update added animal gates and fences and allowed Smart Alarms to sit on other deployables [1]. The Tin Can Alarm can be rigged with grenades and similar items, and the Mortar was added as a raiding and anti-personnel deployable in May 2026 [10].

**Raiding fundamentals.** The wiki lists the satchel charge, timed explosive charge, explosives, beancan and F1 grenades, battering ram, siege tower, catapult and cannon as raiding items [9]. The satchel charge is described as useful for destroying wood and sheet metal doors [11]. The battering ram is a siege weapon for breaking through wooden and stone structures and must be repaired with high quality metal to keep functioning [12]. The Mortar fires shells of two types, one aimed at players and one at structures, fired without a visual guide [10]. Parts of a base whose TC has run dry decay on the timers above, which makes neglected bases weaker targets [2].

**Offline considerations.** The Tool Cupboard wiki page does not address offline behaviour [2]. Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment drawn from the TC, so stocked resources are what protect a base from decay; the page does not tie this to whether owners are online [2]. No Facepunch source on offline raid protection was opened for this document; see Open Questions.

## Guidance 1 — Keep the TC stocked for the material that decays first

- **Guidance:** Stock the TC with more than enough of every material your base uses, prioritising the lowest tier present, because each tier begins to decay on its own timer once its material runs out.
- **Evidence basis:** Upkeep is drawn from the TC and the per-tier decay timers are documented [2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The wiki page is official but undated, and the upkeep rules changed in September 2026 [3].
- **So what:** Check the TC protection timer in game after each monthly update rather than trusting remembered numbers.

## Guidance 2 — Budget for the group upkeep tax before adding teammates

- **Guidance:** Keep the authorised and code-lock player count low, and remove stale guest codes, to avoid a larger upkeep bill.
- **Evidence basis:** The tax is based on players authorised on the TC or a code lock plus those deauthorised in the last 24 hours [3].
- **Confidence:** High. This comes directly from the Facepunch devblog, though server owners may change it [3].
- **So what:** On an unfamiliar server, ask whether the Decay ConVars were changed.

## Guidance 3 — Expect raid costs to drift and verify before planning

- **Guidance:** Use the wiki crafting costs only as a starting point; recheck explosives and tool costs each patch.
- **Evidence basis:** Explosive costs are documented per item [6][11][12], and raid-related items and fixes changed repeatedly in recent updates [1][3][10].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Costs are cited, but the wiki is undated and damage values were not obtained.
- **So what:** Do not plan a raid from a months-old guide.

text:
This deep-dive goes below the foundation document into what it costs to break a base and what defends one: structure and door hit points by tier, explosive damage and sulfur cost, how many explosives each wall or door takes, the upkeep rules that keep a base alive, and the protections that exist in vanilla Rust. The only vanilla protection found in Facepunch sources is the Softcore raid window and TC raid-blocking system added in July 2026 [3], plus the upkeep grace after a TC is destroyed [5].

Confidence is Low. The Facepunch wiki item pages do not list hit points or damage [6][7][8], so the numeric tables come from third-party raid charts that say they were derived from server files or live game data [9][10][11] and that disagree with each other in places. Anything that disagrees is shown side by side and also listed in Open Questions.

- No vanilla offline-raid protection was found in Facepunch sources; offline protection on normal servers appears only as plugins [13] *(assessed from absence of evidence)*.

text:
- **Hard side / soft side:** the outer face of a wall or door versus the interior-facing face, which takes less explosive damage; the soft side is described as the face with the X-shaped braces [9].
- **Raid cost (sulfur):** the raw sulfur needed to craft the explosives used, a standard way third parties compare options [9][10].
- **Honeycomb:** layered walls that multiply the cost of raiding through one side [10].
- **Softcore raid window:** a scheduled period in which raiding is allowed on Softcore servers [3].
- **Group upkeep tax:** the player-count based surcharge on TC upkeep [2].
title: Rust Raiding Costs and Base Defence

text:
**Why counts are not simple division.** C4 is listed at 550 explosion damage but a 500 HP stone wall is listed as needing 2 C4 [9]. The source does not explain the gap; damage falls off with distance, with C4 at full damage at 0 m and zero at 4 m [9]. Treat the per-target counts as the figure to use and the damage numbers as context [9].

**Explosive damage.** The listed profiles are C4 550 explosion; rocket 275 explosion and 75 blunt (full at 1 m, zero at 3.8 m); satchel 75 explosion, 200 blunt and 200 stab; beancan 15 explosion, 50 blunt and 50 stab [9]. The Facepunch wiki pages for C4, satchel and the armoured door do not publish damage or HP; they give recipes, recycling and loot sources only [6][7][8].

**Soft side.** The interior face takes less damage, so fewer explosives are needed. One source gives beancans on a stone wall as 46 from the soft side instead of 64 [9]; another says the soft side takes "roughly half" the explosives without counts [10]. Most calculators default to the hard side [10].

**Weakest-path principle.** Per the charts, the cheapest breach point sets a base's real cost. A sheet metal wall is listed at 4 C4 and a sheet metal door at 1 C4 [9]. A wooden door can be defeated by fire or melee, or one satchel [10].

**Upkeep.** The TC draws a fraction of build cost every 24 hours; the wiki gives no percentages [5]. A 2017 devblog set the fraction by base size (10% for 1 to 15 blocks, up to 33% above 75 blocks) and made it convar-configurable [4]. The September 2026 group tax adds 2% per player for players 5 to 10 and 4% each beyond, capped at 300% [2]. Treat the 2017 percentages as historical only [4].

**Decay and grief protection.** After a material runs out in the TC, parts made of it decay on the timers in Reference Data [5]. A destroyed TC holding resources eats up to 24 hours of upkeep so the base does not decay for 24 hours, designed so a raided player does not lose their base [5]. Raiders can take over the base with their own doors [5].

**Softcore raid windows and raid blocking.** In the Common Ground update (2 July 2026), Softcore raids default to 6 PM to 9 PM server local time. Outside windows, a TC projects a raid-blocking system covering players inside its radius: walls, floors, roofs, doors and ladder hatches cannot be raided. Deployables and an unprotected TC can still be attacked, and the TC must be at least 1 hour old [3]. A third party adds that outside the window explosive and projectile damage on core building parts is blocked while twig, high external walls and gates, and melee stay vulnerable [9]; this was not confirmed against Facepunch text.

**Offline raiding on normal servers.** The Tool Cupboard wiki page does not use the term [5]. Offline protection appears as server plugins: one limits the number of offline raids per player or team per day and per wipe [13]. That is configuration of individual servers, not a vanilla rule [13].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Make the cheapest entry point as expensive as the walls

- **Guidance:** Put your best door tier and any airlock on the shortest path to the TC rather than adding wall layers elsewhere.
- **Evidence basis:** A sheet metal door is listed at 1 C4 while a sheet metal wall is 4, and a honeycomb of three stone layers is 6 C4 [9][10].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The relative counts agree across two charts, but absolute numbers are third-party.
- **So what:** Spend resources on the weakest link first.

## Guidance 2 — Keep the TC stocked and expect it to be targeted

- **Guidance:** Keep upkeep resources in the TC and expect raiders to look for it; a destroyed TC still buys a day of decay protection.
- **Evidence basis:** The Facepunch wiki describes the 24-hour grace and that raiders look for the TC [5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Official page, but undated.
- **So what:** Do not rely on the 24-hour grace to survive an absence; restock after a raid.

## Guidance 3 — On vanilla servers, plan for no offline protection

- **Guidance:** Assume no offline protection unless the server advertises Softcore or a plugin.
- **Evidence basis:** No vanilla offline mechanism was found; only plugins and Softcore windows appear in sources [3][13].
- **Confidence:** Low. This rests on absence of evidence and community plugin pages.
- **So what:** Check server rules and tags before committing to a base location.

## Guidance 4 — Verify counts against the current build before a raid

- **Guidance:** Treat all numbers here as approximations and check an up-to-date calculator or an in-game test.
- **Evidence basis:** Two charts conflict and the Facepunch wiki gives no HP [7][9][10].
- **Confidence:** High. The conflict is directly visible in the cited sources.
- **So what:** Do not budget a raid from a stale chart.

text:
This deep-dive extends the survival overview in rust-game-mechanics-foundation by explaining how damage is dealt and reduced in Rust: per-ammunition base damage and headshot multipliers, how clothing and armour reduce damage by damage type and body area, how melee compares with ranged fire, how bleeding is generated and treated, and what is and is not sourced for explosions and falls. Values were read from the Facepunch Rust Wiki item pages on 2026-10-08, when the Livestock Update (1 October 2026) was the latest update [1].

Document confidence is Medium. Per-item numbers come from Facepunch's own wiki, but the wiki pages omit several mechanics: there is no sourced hit-zone table beyond the headshot multiplier, no sourced fall-damage formula, and no sourced explosion damage numbers. The bleeding formula comes from a single community article that states no build [18]. Those gaps are listed in Open Questions rather than filled from memory.
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
- The Facepunch wiki lists a headshot multiplier of x2 for 5.56 rifle ammunition, pistol ammunition and the Salvaged Sword, x1.5 for Hunting Bow arrows, and x1 to x2 for shotgun ammunition depending on type (checked against the Livestock Update) [3][6][7][8][9].
- Clothing lists the body parts it protects, and damage is reduced according to which body part was hit; clothing does not change hitbox size [2].
- Protection is expressed per damage type: the Metal Facemask lists Projectile 50%, Melee 70% and Explosion 50% for the head slot only [11], and the Hazmat Suit lists 30% projectile, 30% melee and 30% explosion across the full body [13].
- Some clothing has negative protection: the Road Sign Jacket lists Cold -34% [12].
- The Bandage lists Bleeding -50 and Instant Health +5 [14].
- The Livestock Update lists no change to bleeding or fall damage; it did raise the Water Wheel's melee protection and change attack-helicopter armour plates [1].
- No Facepunch source opened for this document gives a fall-damage formula or explosion damage numbers *(assessed from the pages checked; see Open Questions)*.

text:
- **Headshot multiplier:** the factor listed on a weapon's wiki page for head hits [3].
- **Protection:** a per-damage-type percentage listed on a clothing item page [11][12][13].
- **Hit area:** the body part struck, determined by a player collision mesh that does not change with clothing [2].
- **Bleeding:** a status value that causes damage over time [18].
- **Slot and layer:** a clothing item occupies a body slot on the Clothing or Armor layer, for example the Metal Facemask in the Head slot on both layers [11].
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
**Evidence layer.** The hit-area design is from a Facepunch devblog written before the current build, so it is cited as design intent; the numbers come from current wiki pages.

**Hit areas and clothing.** Devblog 117 describes the replacement of mesh-based hitboxes. Previously the exact player model and clothing meshes were colliders, so metal hits did less damage than skin or cloth and results were effectively random in firefights. Under the new system clothing lists the body parts it protects, damage is reduced based on which body part was hit, gloves can add to overall protection, and the struck body part comes from a player collision mesh that does not change with clothing [2]. The same post says per-weapon body-part multipliers were being added, giving the example of higher headshot multipliers for sniper rifles and lower ones for shotguns, and that the direction was undecided [2]. The current wiki headshot values differ by weapon, which is consistent with that design [3][7][8].

**Ranged damage.** The wiki lists damage per ammunition type on each weapon page, with a headshot multiplier. On the Assault Rifle, 5.56 Rifle Ammo, HV and Explosive list 50 damage and Incendiary lists 56, all with x2 [3]. On the Bolt Action Rifle and L96 pages the same four 5.56 types list 80 damage (89.6 Incendiary) with x2 [4][5]. On the Thompson, Pistol Bullet and HV Pistol Ammo list 37.5 and Incendiary lists 42, with x2 [6]. On the Pump Shotgun, 12 Gauge Slug lists 80 with x2, Buckshot 15 with x1.2, Incendiary Shell 15 with x1 and Handmade Shell 9 with x1.2; the page gives no pellet count, so a per-shot total cannot be derived from the wiki [7]. Hunting Bow arrows list Wooden 50, Bone 40, Fire 40 and High Velocity 40, all with x1.5 [8].

**Weapon modifiers.** The Assault Rifle page lists attachment effects: Gas Compression Overdrive (Damage +20%), Military Silencer (Damage -25%), Oil Filter Silencer and Soda Can Silencer (Damage -30%), and Muzzle Brake (Damage -15%) [3].

**Melee.** The Salvaged Sword lists Damage Total 50, Attack Rate 0.8, Headshot Multiplier 2, Range Max 1.5 and Attack Radius 0.3 [9]. The Stone Pickaxe lists Damage Total 17, Attack Rate 1.1, Headshot Multiplier 2, Range Max 1.5 and Attack Radius 0.3 [10]. Both pages also list gather figures against Flesh (Gather Damage 10) [9][10]; the pages do not explain how these relate to combat damage, so they are not interpreted here.

**Protection by damage type.** Clothing pages list percentages per damage type. Metal Facemask: Projectile 50%, Melee 70%, Bite 8%, Cold -4%, Explosion 50%, head only [11]. Road Sign Jacket: Projectile 20%, Melee 20%, Bite 40%, Cold -34%, chest on the Armor layer [12]. Hazmat Suit: Projectile 30%, Melee 30%, Bite 50%, Radiation 50%, Cold 50%, Explosion 30%, full body [13]. The pages opened do not state how multiple items combine, so stacking is not asserted here.

**Bleeding.** The Facepunch wiki lists the Bandage as Bleeding -50, Instant Health +5, Poison -2, and describes it only as healing yourself or a target [14]. A community article states that bleeding equals 20% of damage dealt, ticking 1 damage every 6 seconds until the total is applied, and that bandages or syringes stop it immediately; it gives no build and its related articles are dated December 2024 [18]. The two sources differ on whether a Bandage ends bleeding or subtracts a fixed 50, and the discrepancy is unresolved (see Common Pitfalls).

**Explosions.** The wiki gives crafting data only for the Timed Explosive Charge and Satchel Charge, with no damage figures [16][17]. The Rocket page describes "large splash damage" and gives only rocket counts for structures [15]. The Livestock Update added client prediction when throwing a grenade, C4 or satchel, which affects feel rather than damage [1].

**Falls.** A community FAQ states that fall damage exists and that over 20 damage produces an audible crunch; the page carries no date or build [19]. The Livestock Update lists no fall-damage change [1].

## Guidance 1 — Match armour to the damage type you expect, not to a single protection number

- **Guidance:** Compare protection per damage type and body area before choosing gear, and weigh cold penalties for items such as the Road Sign Jacket.
- **Evidence basis:** Protection is listed per damage type and slot [11][12][13], and some items carry negative values [12].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The item values are primary, but how items stack is unsourced.
- **So what:** A head item with high melee and projectile protection covers only the head [11]; a chest item with low values and a cold penalty can be a poor trade [12].

## Guidance 2 — Treat wiki damage figures as base values, not outcomes

- **Guidance:** Use listed damage and headshot multipliers for relative comparison only.
- **Evidence basis:** Wiki pages list base damage and a multiplier [3][7], protection reduces damage by body area [2][11], and attachments change it [3].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The inputs are primary; the combined result is inference.
- **So what:** Do not expect a listed 50 damage to land as 50 against armoured targets.

## Guidance 3 — Carry more than one bleeding fix until the Bandage behaviour is settled

- **Guidance:** Do not rely on a single Bandage after heavy damage.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki value is -50 [14], and the community article is the only source for the bleed formula [18].
- **Confidence:** Low. The two sources conflict and the formula is single-source.
- **So what:** Check the bleeding value in game after bandaging.

text:
This document is an overview of the core survival loop in Rust (Facepunch Studios, PC): the vital statistics a character must manage (health, hunger, thirst), the environmental pressures (radiation, cold and heat), the helpers (comfort, healing items), the failure states (bleeding, wounded, death), respawn through sleeping bags, the effect of server wipes on progression, and a first look at monuments. Deeper treatment belongs in later deep-dive documents.

The most recent Facepunch update at the time of checking is the Livestock Update of 1 October 2026 [1][2], whose notes list no change to health, hunger, thirst, temperature or respawn mechanics [2]. Item-level numbers come from the Facepunch wiki [3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. Threshold values for hunger, thirst and wounded recovery come only from a community guide [13], so the document-level confidence is Medium: several thresholds have no primary source, and sources conflict on one value.

- **Wounded:** a state entered when a non-lethal hit takes health to zero; the player crawls and may recover or be revived [13].
- **Comfort:** a beneficial effect from being near comfort items [13].
- **Forced wipe:** the monthly wipe that accompanies Facepunch's update [14].
- **Monument:** a pre-generated map landmark with loot and NPCs [15].
title: Rust Game Mechanics: Foundation

text:
**Evidence layer.** Figures marked community-sourced come from a single guide dated 11 June 2026 that states no game build [13].

**Vital stats.** The Facepunch wiki lists consumables as changing hydration, calories and healing over time; for example Water gives Hydration +30 and Healing over time +5, each over 5 seconds [5], and a Can of Beans gives Calories +100, Healing over time +4 and Hydration +25 [8]. A community guide states that a character is dehydrated when hydration falls below about 25, causing slow health and movement-speed loss, and that empty hunger causes steady health loss [13].

**Radiation.** Radiation is picked up in certain areas such as monuments, and higher-tier radiation can still pass through a Hazmat Suit, which gives 50% radiation protection according to a community guide [13]. Anti-Radiation Pills lower radiation and can dehydrate you [6]. Water slightly lowers radiation [5]. A Geiger Counter is a tool item [9]. The Livestock Update fixed Oil Rig radiation starting before the locked crate is looted [2].

**Temperature.** The community guide gives only qualitative cues: nights are colder, snow biomes are harsh, and a wet character gets colder [13]. It gives no numeric temperature thresholds [13]. A Camp Fire "provides warmth and light, and you can cook with it" [10].

**Comfort and regeneration.** Per the community guide, a Campfire roughly doubles the health regeneration tick, a Campfire or running Furnace raises comfort to about 50%, and a chair or Bear Skin Rug can raise it to 100%. Comfort heals only while hunger and hydration are above their low thresholds [13].

**Bleeding, wounded, death.** The Bandage has Instant Health +5 and Bleeding -50 [11]. The Large Medkit removes 100 bleeding, gives +100 healing over time, and guarantees recovery from the wounded state when in the toolbar [7]. Per the guide, wounded recovery takes about 45 seconds before a roll, with a base chance of about 20% and about 45% with maxed food and hydration, and teammates can revive with a Large Medkit or Medical Syringe [13]. Fall damage never causes wounded [13].

**Respawn.** A Sleeping Bag is "a place to respawn, with a long cooldown", is craftable for 30 Cloth, and despawns as a dropped item after 20 minutes [4].

**Wipes and progression.** A forced wipe removes bases, loot and resources and generates a new procedural map; it does not automatically reset blueprints, and blueprint wipes are a server-by-server choice [14]. Facepunch's own wiki documents the scheduled wipe: default Thursday 19:00 London time, with monthly, biweekly or weekly tags [12].

**PvP/PvE loop and monuments (overview).** A community guide describes tiered monuments from Supermarket and Gas Station to Launch Site and Military Tunnels, a three-tier keycard ladder, and hostile NPC scientists and players competing for loot, with Outpost and Bandit Camp as safe zones [15].

This document is the entry point for how Rust turns raw resources into items. It covers gathered resources, crafting, the three workbench tiers, the blueprint and research system, scrap, and the wiki's item categories. It is an overview. Weapon, ammunition and component deep-dives are separate documents.

The core loop is documented by Facepunch: items are locked unless a blueprint is known, workbenches gate tiers, and scrap pays for research [3]. The newest structural change is that workbench levels 2 and 3 need blueprint fragments [2]. Confidence is Medium: the system design rests on Facepunch devblogs, but exact costs come from Rust Wiki item pages that carry no build date, and the October 2026 update was checked only for relevance [1].

text:
**Evidence layer.**

**Locked items and blueprints.** Since Devblog 180 (5 October 2017) all items except default blueprints are locked. Players start with default blueprints such as campfires, furnaces, workbenches and storage [3]. Repairing an item also requires its blueprint [3].

**Research.** A looted item is taken to a research bench and scrap is paid to create a blueprint; the devblog states there is no percentage chance of failure [3]. The wiki states the scrap cost depends on the item's rarity or quality, that blueprints also drop in crates and barrels, and that the table does not check whether you already know the recipe, so scrap can be wasted [10]. Once researched, a blueprint can be studied to permanently learn the recipe [3].

**Workbench experimentation.** Devblog 185 (9 November 2017) added an Experiment UI where scrap produces a random blueprint for that tier that avoids ones already learned [4]. The wiki also notes each workbench has a tech tree for targeting a specific item instead of relying on random drops [10]. The experiment UI was not re-verified against the current build.

**Workbench tiers.** There are three tiers, each requiring the previous tier to craft [3]. Standing near an active workbench lets you craft anything at that tier and below, and crafting is much faster when the bench tier exceeds the item's requirement [3]. Wiki craft times show this: the Research Table takes 30 s at Level 1, 15 s at Level 2, and 7 s at Level 3 [8].

**Fragment gate.** From the Meta Shift update (2 October 2025), Level 2 and 3 workbenches need 5 Basic and 5 Advanced Blueprint Fragments respectively, a stated soft gate pushing players to monuments [2]. The same update says scrap crafting costs for levels 2 and 3 were greatly reduced [2].

**Resources.** Wood is collected from trees and is an ingredient in many recipes [13]. Metal ore and sulfur ore are smelted in furnaces into metal fragments and sulfur [14][15]. Scrap is not craftable and is obtained from loot such as crates, barrels, airdrops and scientists [9]. The October 2026 update added livestock products (milk, wool, meat, bones, leather) as new harvestable resources [1].

**Item categories.** The Rust Wiki groups items into Weapons, Construction, Items, Resources, Attire, Tools, Medical, Food, Ammo, Traps, Components, Electrical, Fun and Misc [16].

This deep-dive goes below the weapons overview in rust-items-crafting-foundation. It lists the main ranged weapons and ammunition types, the workbench level each needs, and the headline stats published on the Facepunch Rust Wiki item pages: craft cost, research cost, damage per ammo type, projectile velocity and headshot multiplier. It does not cover melee, explosives or the combat damage model, which belong to sibling documents.

The headline pattern is a tier ladder. Bows, the crossbow, the Waterpipe Shotgun and the Revolver need no more than Workbench Level 1; the Pump Shotgun, Thompson, Semi-Automatic Pistol and Python need Level 2; the Assault Rifle and Bolt Action Rifle need Level 3 [3][7][8][9][10][11][12][13][16][17]. text:
**Evidence layer.**

**Ammo families.** Each weapon accepts a fixed family. Rifle-calibre weapons take 5.56 Rifle Ammo in four variants: standard, HV, Explosive and Incendiary [3][13]. Pistol-calibre weapons (Revolver, Python, Semi-Automatic Pistol, Thompson) take Pistol Bullet, HV Pistol Ammo and Incendiary Pistol Bullet [7][8][9][12]. Shotguns take 12 Gauge Slug, Buckshot, Incendiary Shell and Handmade Shell [10][11]. Bows and the crossbow share Wooden, Bone, Fire and High Velocity arrows [16][17].

**Variant behaviour.** The wiki describes standard rifle and pistol ammo as losing velocity over distance with slightly reduced damage [4][19]. HV rifle ammo is described as faster, with less drop and slightly higher damage at long range [5]. Explosive rifle ammo explodes on contact for a small amount of fragmentation damage to nearby objects [6]. Per the Assault Rifle page, Incendiary 5.56 lists higher damage (56 versus 50) but lower velocity (225 versus 375), while Explosive lists the same damage as standard with lower velocity [3].

**Workbench gating.** Weapons list a required workbench level, and a higher bench shortens craft time: the Python takes 30 s at Level 2 and 15 s at Level 3 [8]; the Revolver takes 30 s, 15 s and 7 s at Levels 1, 2 and 3 [7].

**Two research prices.** Each item page lists a Research Table price and a "Tech Tree" price at its workbench. For the Revolver these are 30 and 125 Scrap [7]; for the Python 60 and 250 [8]; for the Bolt Action Rifle 120 and 500 [13]. The hunting bow, crossbow and wooden arrow pages state the recipe is known by default, so research is only needed for a physical blueprint for the Industrial Crafter [16][17][18].

**Loot-only weapons.** The M249 page lists the weapon as not craftable and not researchable, with loot from Helicopter and Bradley crates [15]. The LR-300 page lists no craft or research data [14].

text:
Rust servers are modded through third-party frameworks that load C# plugins. The two live frameworks are Oxide (the uMod project, MIT licensed) and Carbon (GPL-3.0, billed as a drop-in Oxide replacement) [1][3][5]. Both were actively releasing on 2026-10-08: Oxide.Rust tag 2.0.7810 on 2026-10-07 and Carbon "Production Build v2.0.262" on 2026-10-02 [2][4].

This document covers what each framework is, how they differ, installation and the permission model, plugin sources and monetisation, and how the Rust server browser classifies modded servers. Confidence is Medium: framework status is primary-sourced, but the uMod licence rules, any explicit Facepunch policy on modded servers and the Oxide install guide pages could not be opened, so those parts rest on indirect sources or are flagged as open questions.

- **Oxide / uMod:** the long-standing Rust modding framework; its docs are at docs.oxidemod.com [7][10].
- **Carbon:** an alternative mod loader, self-updating, using Harmony [1].
- **Plugin:** a C# file placed in the framework's plugins folder (`oxide/plugins` for Oxide) [7].
- **Permission:** a dotted string such as `coolplugin.use` granted to users or groups [11].

text:
**Frameworks.** Oxide is described by the Facepunch wiki as a modding framework letting owners install plugins that change gameplay, such as items, crafting recipes and player behaviour [7]. Carbon describes itself as a self-updating, lightweight mod loader using the latest C# and Harmony, with a permission system, user system and in-game GUI [1].

**Differences (Carbon's own claims).** Carbon says it provides only essential hooks so a server stays close to vanilla, loads only hooks that plugins use, supports hot reload of Harmony mods, has SQL permissions with custom serializers, and an in-game interface for installing and updating plugins [5]. These are vendor claims, not independent benchmarks.

**Installation overview.** Oxide: per the Facepunch wiki, stop the server, run the Oxide installer from the Oxide site, and restart; typing `oxide` in the server console reaches the Oxide console [7]. Oxide's docs home lists dedicated guides for Server Setup, Installing Oxide, Installing Plugins and Permissions [10]. Carbon: download the platform archive from GitHub Releases, extract it to the root of the Rust dedicated server (beside `RustDedicated.exe` on Windows), start the server, and keep server files updated and verified [2][6]. A QuickStart script for Windows and Linux also exists [1].

**Plugin installation.** Plugins are downloaded from the Oxide site or community sites and placed in the `oxide/plugins` folder [7]. Carbon states the same folder structure is retained [5].

**Permissions model.** A practitioner guide documents that uMod creates two groups automatically, `admin` and `default`, that users can be in several groups, and that group permissions supersede individual grants [11]. Each plugin defines its own permission names, so the plugin author's setup notes are authoritative [11].

## Guidance 1 — Pick the framework by plugin set and licence, not by speed claims

- **Guidance:** Choose Oxide when you rely on the broad uMod ecosystem and want the MIT-licensed reference implementation; consider Carbon for its in-game GUI and branch tracking after testing your plugin set on a staging server.
- **Evidence basis:** Both are active and Oxide-plugin-compatible per the vendor [1][2][3][4][5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Compatibility and performance claims come from Carbon's own pages, not independent tests.
- **So what:** Do not migrate a live wipe server without rehearsing every plugin.

## Guidance 2 — Check the framework release before updating Rust

- **Guidance:** Check the framework's latest release for the new Rust build before updating the game server, and expect hook breakage after big updates.
- **Evidence basis:** Oxide shipped a dedicated patch for a Rust hotfix [4]; Carbon ties branches to Rust branches [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Based on two observed release histories.
- **So what:** Schedule updates after the framework release and keep a rollback copy.

## Guidance 3 — Grant plugin permissions to groups, not individuals

- **Guidance:** Manage access through groups with parent inheritance, since group permissions supersede individual grants.
- **Evidence basis:** Practitioner guide on groups and precedence [11].
- **Confidence:** Medium. A single practitioner source, so it cannot exceed Medium.
- **So what:** Fewer stale per-player grants and easier audits.

## Guidance 4 — Read the licence on every paid plugin before buying

- **Guidance:** Treat the marketplace front page as not stating licence terms and ask the author about multi-server use and redistribution.
- **Evidence basis:** Codefling's front page gave no licence terms [12].
- **Confidence:** Low. Absence of terms on one page is weak evidence about the whole marketplace.
- **So what:** Avoid unintended licence breaches when running several servers.

title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
A Rust Oxide plugin is a single C# source file (`.cs`) that the framework compiles at runtime. It holds one public class in the `Oxide.Plugins` namespace, inheriting from `RustPlugin` (or `CovalencePlugin` for game-agnostic plugins), decorated with an `[Info]` attribute for name, author and version [1][2]. Behaviour is added by writing hook methods the framework calls on game events, by registering commands, and by registering permissions [1][2][4][5]. Settings live in a JSON config file in `oxide/config`, persistent state in JSON data files in `oxide/data`, and translated messages in `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` [7][16][17][18].

Carbon, the alternative loader, documents the same plugin shape: `RustPlugin` in `Oxide.Plugins` for Oxide-compatible plugins, and `CarbonPlugin` in `Carbon.Plugins` for Carbon-only plugins [19]. Where Carbon differs (hook dispatch, extra command attributes, config folder name) this document labels the difference only where a Carbon page states it [20][21][23]. Confidence is Medium: structure and API are primary-sourced from the framework docs, but several pages are thin (no signatures on the core permission library page, no description on some hook pages), and the Oxide docs say nothing on how conflicting hook return values from several plugins are resolved.
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
- Oxide plugins are distributed as `.cs` files; extensions are `.dll` files [1][2].
- The main class is public, lives in `Oxide.Plugins` and inherits `RustPlugin` for Rust-only plugins [2]. The plugin guidelines say the file name should match the main class name in PascalCase [8].
- Metadata is `[Info("Name", "Author", "1.0.0")]` plus an optional `[Description("...")]` [2][4][8].
- Lifecycle order is Init, Loaded, OnServerInitialized, then (on shutdown) Shutdown and Unload [3].
- For hooks documented with return behaviour, a non-null return overrides default behaviour and null lets it proceed (`CanLootEntity`); many hooks list "No return behavior" [12][13][14][15].
- Oxide's hook index grouped hooks into 38 categories on 2026-10-08, the largest being Player (155), Entity (102), Item (64) and Vehicle (52) [11].
- Permissions are registered with `permission.RegisterPermission(name, this)`, and the documented convention is `pluginname.permission` in lowercase [5][8].
- Carbon says its folder and plugin structure matches Oxide, but Oxide's `config` folder becomes `configs` and commands use a `c.` prefix instead of `o.` [23][28].

Covered: structure and APIs of server-side C# plugins for Rust on Oxide (uMod) and Carbon: class and attributes, lifecycle, hooks and their return semantics, commands, permissions API, config, data files and localization files, development environment, and official authoring guidelines. Build: Oxide.Rust 2.0.7810 and Carbon v2.0.262 era (Rust 2634.289.1, October 2026).

Not covered: installing frameworks and the admin-side permission commands (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation), individual plugin reviews, the Rust game systems hooks touch (see rust-combat-damage-model, rust-weapons-ammo, rust-raiding-costs-defence), console and client modification, and Carbon module/UI libraries beyond a mention.
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
- **Hook:** a function called by the game or by Oxide to define what happens on a game event [1].
- **Info attribute:** the metadata attribute carrying plugin name, author and version [2][4].
- **Covalence plugin:** a game-agnostic plugin deriving from `CovalencePlugin`, versus a `RustPlugin` for Rust only [2].
- **Data file:** JSON persistence in `oxide/data`, distinct from the admin-edited config in `oxide/config` [7][17].
- **Harmony patch:** a runtime method patch installed with `[AutoPatch]` plus `[HarmonyPatch]`, available in both frameworks' docs [4][20].
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
**Plugin file and class.** A plugin is one `.cs` file compiled at runtime; the beginner guide names both file and class `MyFirstPlugin`, uses the `Oxide.Plugins` namespace, and derives from `RustPlugin` [2]. The guidelines state the file name "should match the name of your main class and use PascalCase" [8]. Carbon's first-plugin page uses the file-scoped namespace form (`namespace Oxide.Plugins;`) for Oxide-compatible plugins [19]. Compile errors appear in the server console after the file is uploaded [2].

**Development environment.** Oxide's guide names Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code and JetBrains Rider as IDE options, and lists `Oxide.Core.dll`, `Oxide.Rust.dll`, `Assembly-CSharp.dll` and `UnityEngine.dll` as the references to add [10]. Its best-practices page recommends Git source control (excluding binaries, logs and local config), testing, and documenting installation, commands and configuration [9]. For Carbon, the developer docs describe a local Windows development server built from the Carbon.QuickStart files, with an optional debugger set in `doorstop_config.ini` [25].

**Attributes.** `[Info("Name", "Author", "1.0.0")]`: the name uses spaces between words, the second argument is the developer or maintainer, and the version is three-part [4]. `[Description]` is a brief summary [4]; the guidelines recommend it for documentation [8]. Further documented attributes: `[ChatCommand]`, `[ConsoleCommand]`, `[Command]` (covalence), `[Permission]`, `[PluginReference]`, `[OnlinePlayers]`, `[HookMethod("HookName")]` and `[AutoPatch]`; comment directives `//Requires: PluginName` (plugin will not start if the required plugin is missing) and `//Reference: AssemblyName` [4].

**Lifecycle.** Per Oxide's lifecycle page: `Init` runs first, before dependencies are available, and an exception there stops initialisation; `Loaded` runs after Init and before registration, and is where asynchronously loaded config and localisation can be read through the `Config` object; `OnServerInitialized` runs near the end of boot, and still runs locally on a runtime reload; `Shutdown` runs only if the game provider supports Advanced Hooks; `Unload` runs when the plugin manager unloads the plugin. `OnConfigChanged` can override default config monitoring during hotloading [3]. The beginner guide registers permissions in `Init` [2][5]; the hook page shows `OnServerInitialized(bool serverInitialized)` is called with `true` after startup and with `false` on hot-loaded plugins when the server is already initialised [13].

**Hooks.** Hooks are methods whose name and parameters match a documented hook; the framework calls them when the event fires [1][2]. Each hook has its own page at `/hooks/<category>/<HookName>` giving signature, description where present, return behaviour and the engine call site [11][12]. For `CanLootEntity(BasePlayer player, WorldItem instance)`, the page states that returning a non-null value overrides default behaviour and returning null lets it proceed [12]. Other documented hooks list "No return behavior" (`OnServerInitialized`, `OnUserPermissionGranted`, `OnPlayerConnected`) [13][14][15]. `OnUserPermissionGranted` fires only when the permission is newly added to the user's data [14]. Hook names often come in pairs (for example `OnOvenStart`/`OnOvenStarted`), which is an inference from names, not stated by the index [11].

**Commands.** Rust plugins use `[ChatCommand("name")]` with `(BasePlayer player, string command, string[] args)` and `[ConsoleCommand("name")]` with `(ConsoleSystem.Arg arg)`; covalence plugins use `[Command]` with an `IPlayer` [4]. `[Permission("perm.name")]` restricts a command to holders of that permission [4]. The guidelines ask for lowercase underscore command names such as `my_command` [8].

**Permissions API (Oxide).** Register in `Init` with `permission.RegisterPermission("epicstuff.use", this)`; check with `permission.UserHasPermission("playerID", "epicstuff.use")` or `player.HasPermission(...)` on an `IPlayer`; group management includes `CreateGroup(name, title, rank)`, `GrantGroupPermission`, `RevokeGroupPermission`, `GetGroupPermissions(group, includeParents)`, `AddUserGroup` and `UserHasGroup` [5]. The beginner guide passes `player.UserIDString` to `UserHasPermission` [2]. The core library page confirms `RegisterPermission` makes a permission available for assignment to players and groups, and that `CreateGroup` attaches group title and rank [6].

**Config, data and lang files.** Config lives in `oxide/config/<PluginName>.json` and is the admin-edited layer; data lives in `oxide/data` and is plugin-managed; language files are `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` [7][16][17][18]. A data file is opened with `Interface.Oxide.DataFileSystem.GetFile(Name)`, returning a `DynamicConfigFile` with `ReadObject<T>()`, `WriteObject(obj)` and `Clear()` [7]. Classes are serialised with Newtonsoft.Json; `[JsonProperty(PropertyName=...)]` sets a readable key, `[JsonIgnore]` excludes runtime fields, and `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` on lists prevents default entries accumulating on every restart [7]. The beginner guide implements config through `LoadConfig`, `LoadDefaultConfig`, `GetDefaultConfig` and `SaveConfig` [2]. The Oxide docs do not describe how plugin code registers messages; admin-facing notes only describe the file layout, `{0}`/`{1}` placeholders and Rust text tags [18].

**Carbon plugin shape.** Carbon documents the same layout for Oxide-compatible plugins and a Carbon-only variant: namespace `Carbon.Plugins`, base class `CarbonPlugin` [19]. Carbon's hook system differs internally: it calls hooks by numeric ID through `HookCaller.CallStaticHook` rather than `Interface.CallHook` with a name string [20]. Its owner-facing comparison says Carbon only runs hooks that loaded plugins need, while Oxide "fires all hooks all the time" (Carbon's wording) [23]. Carbon's hooks reference marks hooks not flagged Static or Patch as applied dynamically when a plugin subscribes [24]. Carbon adds command restriction attributes `[Group]`, `[AuthLevel(n)]` and `[Cooldown(ms)]` beside `[Permission]`, plus `[ProtectedCommand]` [21].

|---------|-----------------------|--------|
| Namespace | `Oxide.Plugins` | [2][19] |
| Base class | `RustPlugin` (Rust) or `CovalencePlugin` (game-agnostic) | [2] |

| Hook method | `private void OnServerInitialized()` style | [13][19] |
| Config file | `oxide/config/<Plugin>.json` | [16] |
| Data files | `oxide/data/` (subfolder per plugin recommended) | [7][17] |
| Lang file | `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` | [7][18] |

Lifecycle sequence [3]:

| Order | Step | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| 1 | `Init` | Before dependencies available; exception rolls back |
| 2 | `Loaded` | Read async config/localisation via `Config` |
| 3 | `OnServerInitialized` | Boot nearly complete; runs on hot reload too |
| 4 | `Shutdown` | Only with Advanced Hooks support |
| 5 | `Unload` | After hook routing disabled |

Documented hook examples (Oxide hook pages, 2026-10-08):

| Hook | Signature | Return behaviour | Source |
|------|-----------|------------------|--------|
| `CanLootEntity` | `object CanLootEntity(BasePlayer, WorldItem)` | Non-null overrides default; null proceeds | [12] |
| `OnServerInitialized` | `void OnServerInitialized(bool)` | None | [13] |
| `OnUserPermissionGranted` | `void (string playerId, string permission)` | None | [14] |
| `OnPlayerConnected` | `void (BasePlayer)` | None | [15] |

Oxide hook index category counts (2026-10-08) [11]:

| Category | Hooks | Category | Hooks |
|----------|-------|----------|-------|
| Player | 155 | Server | 46 |
| Entity | 102 | Structure | 33 |
| Item | 64 | Weapon | 25 |
| Vehicle | 52 | Permission | 13 |

Command attributes [4][21]:

| Attribute | Scope | Signature | Framework |
|-----------|-------|-----------|-----------|
| `[ChatCommand]` | Chat | `(BasePlayer, string, string[])` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[ConsoleCommand]` | F1/terminal/RCon | `(ConsoleSystem.Arg)` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[Command]` | Chat and console | Oxide: `(IPlayer, string, string[])`; Carbon: `(BasePlayer, string, string[])` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[Group]`, `[AuthLevel]`, `[Cooldown]`, `[ProtectedCommand]` | Restrictions | n/a | Carbon docs only [21] |

Permission API calls [5][22]:

| Call | Oxide docs | Carbon docs |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| `RegisterPermission(name, plugin)` | Yes [5] | Yes; in `Init()` or `OnServerInitialized()` [22] |
| `UserHasPermission(id, name)` | Yes [5] | Yes [22] |
| `CreateGroup(name, title, rank)` | Yes [5] | Yes; returns false if exists [22] |
| `GetGroupPermissions(group, parents)` | Yes [5] | Yes [22] |
| `AddUserGroup` / `UserHasGroup` | Yes [5] | Not documented on the page [22] |

Naming rules from the Oxide plugin guidelines [8]: commands lowercase with underscores; permissions `pluginname.permission` with lowercase plugin name; locals camelCase; properties PascalCase; semantic versioning with the `[Info]` version updated on every change.

Carbon versus Oxide migration facts, as stated by Carbon [23]:

| Item | Carbon statement |
|------|------------------|
| Coexistence | Oxide and Carbon cannot run on the same install |
| Command prefix | `c.` instead of `o.` |
| Config folder | Oxide `config` becomes `carbon/configs` |
| Plugin source changes | Page does not describe any required |
| Permission storage | Carbon says it uses SQLite-based permissions |

text:
- Treating `Init` as safe for dependencies: the lifecycle page says dependencies are not available in `Init`, and an exception there rolls back compilation [3].
- Config overwritten on unload: some plugins save config when unloaded, so edits made while loaded can be lost; the admin guidance is to unload, edit, load [16].
- Default list entries piling up on restart unless `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` is set [7].
- Missing `//Requires:` dependency: the plugin will not start [4].
- Returning a value from a hook with documented "No return behavior" has no documented effect; returning non-null from override-style hooks blocks default behaviour [12][13].
- Blocking the main thread with heavy computation or file I/O is called out as disrespectful to the server in the guidelines [8].
- Assuming Carbon and Oxide can be mixed: Carbon states they cannot coexist [23]. Carbon also says it needs unmodified Facepunch DLLs, so Oxide-patched files must be reverted [23].
- Typing `o.` commands on Carbon: they do not work, though aliases can be defined [23].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Register permissions early and name them pluginname.action

- **Guidance:** Register every permission in `Init` (or `OnServerInitialized` on Carbon), use lowercase `pluginname.action` names, and gate commands with `[Permission]` rather than hand-written checks where possible.
- **Evidence basis:** Registration in `Init` and the naming convention are documented [2][5][8][22]; the `[Permission]` attribute is documented [4][21].
- **Confidence:** High. Several primary pages from both frameworks agree.
- **So what:** Admins can find and grant the permission with standard commands, and permissions do not collide across plugins.

## Guidance 2 — Keep Init minimal and defer cross-plugin work to OnServerInitialized

- **Guidance:** Do setup that needs other plugins or world state in `OnServerInitialized`, and handle both `true` and `false` values of its parameter so hot reloads behave.
- **Evidence basis:** Init runs before dependencies are available; OnServerInitialized runs on reload with `false` [3][13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The lifecycle page is clear but the advice is a synthesis, and no primary page tests it.
- **So what:** Fewer load-order bugs when a plugin is reloaded on a live server.

## Guidance 3 — Separate config from data and guard against list accumulation

- **Guidance:** Put admin-tunable settings in the config and plugin-managed state in data files, and set `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` on default lists.
- **Evidence basis:** Config/data split and the list behaviour [7][16][17].
- **Confidence:** High. Stated on official pages.
- **So what:** Admins edit the right file, backups cover `oxide/data`, and restarts do not duplicate default entries.

## Guidance 4 — Write for Oxide compatibility unless you need Carbon-only features

- **Guidance:** Use `RustPlugin` and `Oxide.Plugins` by default, and use `CarbonPlugin` or Carbon-only command attributes only when you accept losing Oxide portability.
- **Evidence basis:** Carbon documents both shapes and labels Carbon-only attributes [19][21]; Carbon says the plugin structure is the same [28].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Compatibility is the framework's own claim, and the docs do not test every attribute across both.
- **So what:** A single plugin file can serve servers on either framework; test on both before claiming support.

## Guidance 5 — Re-verify every hook signature against the current hook page before shipping

- **Guidance:** Treat a hook's signature and return behaviour as build-specific and check the hook page after each Rust update.
- **Evidence basis:** Oxide shipped a patch for a Rust hotfix and added new hooks the same day [26]; hook pages list the engine call site [12].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The release evidence is two observed releases.
- **So what:** Fewer silently dead hooks after a Rust update.

text:
This document is the entry point for running a Rust dedicated server: installing it through SteamCMD, opening ports, choosing launch parameters, using `server.cfg`, generating a map, wiping on schedule, administering through RCON and auth levels, and staying inside Facepunch's server guidelines. It stays at overview depth and points to the Facepunch wiki pages that hold the detail.

Confidence is Medium. Most install, port, wipe and ban facts come from the Facepunch wiki and Facepunch's own guidelines and devblogs, which are primary. However, several wiki pages are old or thin (RCON, convar defaults and anti-cheat configuration are not documented in the pages read), so those areas are stated narrowly and flagged as open questions. Checked against the October 2026 update [8].
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text:
- The Rust dedicated server is Steam app id 258550, installed with SteamCMD using an anonymous login [1].
- The game port is UDP 28015 by default, the query port is UDP and must differ from the game port, and RCON is TCP [1].
- `server.cfg` lives in `rust/server/server.identity/cfg/`, is read at startup, overrides command-line settings, and is never rewritten by the server [1].
- The default wipe schedule is the first Thursday of the month at 19:00 London time, aligned with Facepunch forced wipes [2].
- `ownerid` grants auth level 2 and `moderatorid` grants auth level 1 [7].
- Facepunch's Community Server and Hosting Guidelines (updated 15 July 2025) permit several monetisation methods but forbid granting Facepunch DLC to players who do not own it [3].
- Servers can require TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot; Facepunch reported fewer cheaters on its secure servers [9][8].
- A mandatory server and client update was announced for 22 October 2026 at 18:00 BST [8].

text:
- **SteamCMD** — Valve's command-line Steam client used to download the server files [1].
- **server identity** — a named folder holding one server's saves, config and admin files, so one install can run several servers [5].
- **Auth level** — admin permission tier: 2 owner, 1 moderator [7].
- **RCON** — remote console used to run server commands over the network [1].
- **Forced wipe** — Facepunch's monthly update-day wipe that a new protocol version makes necessary [2][5].
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text:
**Install.** The server app id is 258550. The wiki gives the Linux form `./steamcmd.sh +force_install_dir ../rust +login anonymous +app_update 258550 validate +quit`. Omitting `+login` yields "No subscription". Beta branches are installed with `-beta <branch>` (for example `staging`). After testing a higher build, return to the `public` branch or delete the steamapps folder [1].

**Ports.** `server.port` (UDP, default 28015) and `server.queryport` (UDP) must both be open. If `queryport` is unset it defaults to one more than the higher of `server.port` or `rcon.port`, and it must differ from `server.port`. `rcon.port` is TCP and Rust+ also uses a TCP port; RCON and Rust+ ports are needed only if those features are wanted [1].

**Launch parameters and server.cfg.** Common launch arguments are `-batchmode`, `+server.port`, `+server.level "Procedural Map"`, `+server.seed`, `+server.worldsize`, `+server.maxplayers`, `+server.ip`, `+rcon.port`, `+rcon.password`, `+rcon.web 1` and `-logfile`. `server.cfg` takes the same settings without the `+`/`-` prefix, is read at start-up, overrides the command line, and is never edited by the server itself. Some variables (for example weather chance settings) can only be set once the server is running [1]. The command `server.writecfg` writes current convars to the cfg files [7].

**Map generation.** The wiki describes procedural maps with a seed (0 to 2147483647) and world size (the wiki suggests 1000 to 6000; larger maps need more disk and memory) [1]. Procedural maps are saved as `proceduralmap.SIZE.SEED.map` [5]. A JSON file loaded with `+world.configfile` can switch off roads, rivers, powerlines and underwater labs or blacklist/whitelist prefabs; it applies only when a map is first generated, so existing maps need the `.map` file deleted [4].

**Saves and wipes.** The `.sav` file holds entities, buildings and deployables, and the protocol number in its name increases at a forced wipe so the server starts a new file; a blueprint wipe also requires deleting `player.blueprints` [5]. The wipe timer defaults to the first Thursday monthly at 19:00 London time, with weekly and biweekly options, controlled by `wipetimer.wipeDayofWeek`, `wipetimer.wipeHourofDay`, `wipetimer.wipeTimezone`, `wipetimer.wipeUnixTimestampOverride` and `wipetimer.wipeCronOverride`; the `PrintWipe` command shows the calculated schedule [2].

**Administration.** `users` lists players with Steam64 IDs; `ownerid <steamid> "<name>"` and `moderatorid <steamid> "<name>"` grant auth levels 2 and 1; `removeowner` revokes level 2; the player must reconnect to receive the level [1][7]. `kick` and `ban` (with optional duration such as `1M7d5m`) are available to admins [7]. An optional centralized ban list is enabled by pointing `server.bansServerEndpoint` at a self-hosted HTTP API; it blocks joins but does not kick players already online [6].

**Rules and anti-cheat.** Facepunch's guidelines allow a server fee or subscription, donations, cosmetics and enhancements, a server currency, and adverts or sponsorships. Facepunch DLC must be available to players who own it and must not be granted to those who do not; only test servers are excepted. Enforcement can include delisting, other sanctions or a game ban, and cheating, griefing or hacking are prohibited [3]. The guidelines name no specific anti-cheat tool [3]. Facepunch announced that servers can require TPM and Secure Boot [8][9].

## Guidance 1 — Keep the wipe schedule at its default unless you have a reason

- **Guidance:** Leave the wipe timer on the default first-Thursday 19:00 London schedule and use the override convars only for deliberate off-cycle wipes.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki says the default aligns with forced wipes and rarely needs changing [2], and the save filename protocol changes at forced wipes [5].
- **Confidence:** High. Both statements are first-party Facepunch documentation.
- **So what:** A schedule that disagrees with the forced wipe invites a mid-cycle wipe or a broken save.

## Guidance 2 — Re-check launch arguments and convars after every monthly update

- **Guidance:** After each update, read the devblog server section and re-test launch arguments and `server.cfg` before opening the server to players.
- **Evidence basis:** Convars were added, changed and removed in consecutive updates [8][9], and the install page flags outdated content [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is documented, but how often a given setting breaks is inference.
- **So what:** Reading the notes avoids silent behaviour changes and covers the announced 22 October mandatory update [8].

## Guidance 3 — Decide monetisation and DLC policy before launch

- **Guidance:** If you sell anything, keep to the listed methods and never unlock Facepunch DLC for non-owners.
- **Evidence basis:** The guidelines list permitted methods and the DLC prohibition, with enforcement up to a game ban [3].
- **Confidence:** High. The source is Facepunch's own legal text, though only the live page is authoritative.
- **So what:** Breaching it risks delisting or bans for the operator.

## Guidance 4 — Weigh secure mode and set a strong RCON password

- **Guidance:** Evaluate TPM and Secure Boot requirements as a cheat deterrent, accepting that a share of players cannot meet them, and never leave the placeholder RCON password.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch's figures show fewer cheaters on secure servers but only about 60% of players qualifying [9]; the wiki tells admins to change the RCON password [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The cheater figure comes from a six-server sample reported by Facepunch.
- **So what:** Stricter entry trades population for fewer cheaters.

text:
This reference lists the server convars that Facepunch itself documents or names, grouped by purpose: startup and world, decay and upkeep, Rust+ companion, secure-server and encryption, tags and gamemodes, and recent devblog additions. It goes deeper than rust-server-administration-foundation by giving names, defaults and effects row by row, and by resolving the foundation's open question on secure-server convars.

Confidence is Medium. Every row comes from a Facepunch wiki page or devblog, but Facepunch publishes no complete convar list, many pages are marked as old or work in progress, and several defaults are simply not stated. Gather-rate convars and the RCON connection-limit convar names were not found on any Facepunch page and are listed as gaps rather than guessed. Checked against the October 2026 update [6].
title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text:
- Facepunch's wiki documents only a handful of decay convars: `decay.scale` (default 1), `decay.upkeep_period_minutes` (default 1440) and `decay.upkeep_grief_protection` (default 1440) [1].
- `server.useServerWideRequiredSystemConfig` requires TPM and Secure Boot for all players and earns the Secure browser tag; `server.usePerPlayerRequiredSystemConfig` enforces per player and does not earn the tag [8].
- `server.secure` was removed on 4 September 2025; insecure servers now pass `-insecure` at startup, and a secure server needs `server.encryption` set to 2 [9][10].
- `app.port` defaults to the larger of game port or RCON port plus 67 (28082 with default ports), must be 10000 or higher, and `-1` disables Rust+ [3].
- `rcon.port` is TCP and `server.queryport` is UDP and must differ from `server.port` [5].
- `UsePlayerUpdateJobs` has defaulted to 2 since the April 2026 update [7].
- No Facepunch page opened for this document lists a gather-rate convar or any default for one *(gap, see Open Questions)*.
- The Useful Console Commands page says it is a work in progress and last updated "A Long Time Ago" [1].

text:
- **Convar** — a console variable or command that configures the server; set at launch, in `server.cfg`, or at runtime [5].
- **Upkeep** — resources a Tool Cupboard consumes to protect a base from decay [2].
- **Secure tag** — server-browser tag shown only when TPM and Secure Boot are enforced for all players [8].
- **Companion server** — the Rust+ listener configured with the `app.*` convars [3].

text:
**Setting convars.** Launch arguments use `+name value`; `server.cfg` in `server/<identity>/cfg/` takes the same settings without the prefix. For settings not in the wiki table the page suggests the `find` console command, for example `find image` [5]. The foundation document covers file locations and precedence.

**Decay and upkeep.** A Tool Cupboard pays upkeep, described as a fraction of the resources used to build, per 24 hours. With no resources in a cupboard, decay starts immediately. Decay starts at the outermost exposed pieces and moves inward, and if one upkeep material runs out only parts of that material decay [2]. After upkeep runs out, the wiki gives full-decay times: twig 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours. A destroyed cupboard that held resources consumes up to 24 hours of upkeep, protecting the base for that long [2]. The tool-cupboard page names no convars and carries no build date [2]; the console-commands page supplies the three decay convars [1]. Vehicle decay is separate: minicopter, attack and transport helicopters have their own inside and outside decay timers [1].

**Rust+ companion.** `app.port` sets the listening port and `-1` disables Rust+ (on the command line this is written `+app.port 1-` because of parser conflicts). The server must reach companion-rust.facepunch.com. `app.listenip` selects the NIC, `app.publicip` sets the address the app uses when `app.info` shows a wrong one, and `app.id` carries a warning not to change it [3].

**Secure servers and encryption.** From 5 March 2026 servers can opt in to requiring TPM and Secure Boot [8]. From 7 August 2025 an insecure server is started with `-insecure` rather than `server.secure false` [9]; on 4 September 2025 Facepunch removed `server.secure` and required `server.encryption` 2 for a server to count as secure [10]. The pages opened do not mention Easy Anti-Cheat settings [6][8][9][10].

**Tags and gamemodes.** `server.tags` takes a comma-separated list (example `weekly,vanilla,roleplay`), `server.pve` applies the PvE tag, up to four tags show at once, and tags in the same group should not be combined [11]. `server.gamemode` sets a gamemode at startup, empty meaning default gameplay [4].

## Guidance 1 — Treat the wiki convar defaults as starting points and verify with `find`

- **Guidance:** Before relying on any default in this table, confirm the live value with the server console `find` command after each monthly update.
- **Evidence basis:** The console-commands page is work in progress and old [1], the wiki itself recommends `find` for unlisted settings [5], and convars change monthly [6][7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The staleness of the pages is documented; how many defaults have drifted is not known.
- **So what:** Avoids trusting a stale default when tuning decay or ports.

## Guidance 2 — Change decay with `decay.scale` first

- **Guidance:** To make a server more or less punishing about decay, adjust `decay.scale` before touching the upkeep period, and record any change in the server description.
- **Evidence basis:** `decay.scale` is the single documented multiplier, while the upkeep convars shift only cost timing and grief protection [1]; material decay times are documented separately [2].
- **Confidence:** Low. The ordering is inference, and the effect of the scale on each material time is not documented.
- **So what:** A single multiplier is easier to reason about and revert than three interacting values.

## Guidance 3 — Use server-wide secure enforcement only if you accept the population cost

- **Guidance:** Enable `server.useServerWideRequiredSystemConfig` only if reduced cheating matters more than losing players without TPM and Secure Boot.
- **Evidence basis:** Enforcement and the tag are documented [8], and Facepunch reported that roughly 60% of players have the features enabled [7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The mechanism is first-party; the trade-off is judgement.
- **So what:** Expect a smaller pool of eligible players in return for the Secure tag.

## Guidance 1 — Expect the next content update on Thursday 5 November 2026, but confirm it

- **Guidance:** Plan for a monthly update on the first Thursday of November (5 November 2026) after the 22 October Halloween Update, and treat the date as unconfirmed until Facepunch posts it.
- **Evidence basis:** Nine consecutive first-Thursday update posts from February to October [1][2]; the stated monthly plan [3]; the announced 22 October Halloween Update [14].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is solid, but the January post warned some months may be light and Facepunch has not announced November.
- **So what:** Admins schedule mod and wipe preparation for 5 November while watching the news index, and players treat the date as likely rather than guaranteed.

## Guidance 2 — Read experimental toggles as short-lived

- **Guidance:** Do not build long-term server configuration on features flagged experimental or opt-in in a given month.
- **Evidence basis:** Jobs levels moved from experimental to default within months [9][11][12]; the Rust Render Pipeline toggle is stated to last the first month [14]; the navmesh was opt-in in June and still being tested in September [10][13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is documented across several posts, but whether each feature ships is unknown.
- **So what:** Re-check the devblog each month before relying on an experimental convar.

It covers how to read a devblog, which Steam branches exist for testing, how game modes such as softcore differ from vanilla, platform and licence facts, and a timeline of the eight most recent monthly updates (March to October 2026) read directly from Facepunch.

Document-level confidence is Medium. The monthly cadence and the devblog contents are directly verified from primary Facepunch sources. The exact force-wipe hour, the console edition's current schedule, and the purpose of non-staging branches rest on a community wiki, secondary reporting, or could not be confirmed.

text:
**Cadence.** The Facepunch news index lists a devblog on the first Thursday of every month from March to October 2026 [1]. Wikipedia reports that after leaving Early Access the update cycle moved from weekly to monthly, citing PC Gamer [14]. The Facepunch wiki gives the default monthly wipe as the first Thursday at 19:00 London time and notes defaults align with force wipes [11].

**Reading a devblog.** Posts are titled with a theme name and dated; the page contains headline features, followed by a changelist (the "Breach and Clear" post is labelled the September Update Changelist, and "Power Trip" gives changelist 4044) [3][4]. Convar names and launch parameters appear inline, for example `vehicle.padrepairsrequired` [2], `antihack.parenthistory` [6], and the opt-in `-useNewNavmesh` parameter [3]. Experimental or opt-in features are flagged in the text, such as the Rust Render Pipeline toggle [2]. Wipe-relevant behaviour is usually stated in terms of "the wipe" rather than a dated force wipe [2][6]. Non-update news posts exist and are not devblogs, for example the Lunar New Year post [10].

**Branches.** The Facepunch wiki says beta branches let you test features not released to the public, using SteamCMD against app ID 258550, with `staging` and `aux01` as the documented examples; moving back requires specifying `public` [12]. The "Shipshape" post mentions data from an "EU Staging server" [9]. The purpose of aux01 beyond testing is not stated in the sources opened.

**Modes and server types.** The "Common Ground" update documents Softcore changes (2x resource gather multiplier, scheduled raid windows defaulting to 6 PM to 9 PM server time with Tool Cupboard raid blocking outside them) and notes the clan system is disabled in hardcore mode [5]. The wiki's server page lists a "Gamemodes" topic under server hosting [15]. Community servers set their own wipe timing; the wiki exposes `wipeDayofWeek`, `wipeHourofDay`, `wipeTimezone` and cron overrides for the in-game wipe timer [11].

**Platform and licence.** Steam lists Facepunch Studios as developer and publisher, with a release date of 8 February 2018 and Windows and macOS support [13]. Early Access began December 2013 and ended 8 February 2018 [14]. The Steam page does not state an Early Access status, only a user tag [13]. Console editions for PS4 and Xbox One launched 21 May 2021 with Double Eleven; PS5 and Xbox Series X/S early access began 19 June 2025 with full release 26 June 2025; the PS4/Xbox One versions were delisted 29 May 2025 and their servers shut in October 2025 [14].

## Guidance 1 — Plan around the first Thursday and re-verify details each month

- **Guidance:** Treat the first Thursday of each month as update and wipe day, and recheck the devblog for that month before relying on any value in this knowledge base.
- **Evidence basis:** Eight consecutive devblogs on first Thursdays [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]; wiki defaults aligned with force wipes [11].
- **Confidence:** High. The pattern is directly observed in primary sources for eight months and matches the wiki.
- **So what:** Players schedule wipe-day play for the first Thursday; admins plan mod updates the same day.

## Guidance 2 — Admins should pin the branch and expect plugin lag

- **Guidance:** Run the public branch for live servers, use staging or aux01 only on a test server, and delay the wipe-day launch until the framework you use has updated.
- **Evidence basis:** Branch commands and the Oxide reinstall warning [12]; the staging server reference [9].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The commands are documented but the stability of each branch is not stated in the sources opened.
- **So what:** A test server on staging catches plugin breakage before wipe day.

## Guidance 3 — Check the specific mode before quoting rates or rules

- **Guidance:** Do not assume vanilla values apply on softcore or modded servers; verify the mode first.
- **Evidence basis:** Softcore 2x gather and raid windows [5]; wipe timer configurable by hosts [11].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Mode behaviour is documented for softcore only; other modes were not verified.
- **So what:** Guides quoting vanilla numbers can be wrong on community servers.
